articles.title_orig: Putin says Russia won't negotiate limited ceasefire with Ukraine after bridge strike
articles.title_zh: Putin says Russia won't negotiate limited ceasefire with Ukraine after bridge strike
articles.content_orig:
President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that Russia will not negotiate with Ukraine on a limited ceasefire, citing a Ukrainian strike this week on a major bridge connecting Russia and Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Putin made the remarks to reporters in Russian after meeting with President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China. He said he had discussed the possibility of a ceasefire in certain areas of Ukraine, but would not move forward with negotiations after Ukraine's strike on the Kerch Bridge, according to the Russian state news agencies.
The 12-mile bridge, which Putin ceremonially opened himself in 2018, is hugely symbolic as it links the Russian mainland with Crimea — territory that Russian forces occupied about four years earlier. The missile strike this week wasn't the first time Ukraine had targeted the piece of infrastructure, but it inflicted severe damage. Russia also struck two major bridges in Kyiv the same day.
Putin played down the bridge's strategic importance on Thursday and said he had heard the calls "from all sides" for a naval ceasefire or a suspension of strikes on energy facilities, but he ruled out direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing the attack on the bridge.
"Honestly, I discussed the issue with my colleagues at the Security Council, and I asked them to think about it and go back to the issue, so that we could reach some agreements," Putin said, according to Russian state news agency TASS. "However, we will not make agreements after strikes on the Crimean Bridge. We will respond to these strikes."
Putin vowed that Russia's retaliation for the strike on the bridge would be severe, TASS reported.
While Putin claims frequently to want peace, he denies that Russia started the war with his order for a full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, and Russia's attacks on Ukraine have been relentless.
It's not clear how much Ukraine came up in Mr. Trump's one-on-one meeting with Putin on Wednesday, or in the meeting with both Putin and Xi on Thursday. Last week, the White House said Ukraine wouldn't be a topic of discussion, but before he left for Asia, Mr. Trump said the three leaders would be discussing the war. The White House readout of the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting was sparse on detail, and did not mention Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff have been in Germany to meet with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other European leaders about Ukraine and other topics.
Kushner said they discussed the "latest efforts to achieve a just, lasting and durable peace in Ukraine."
"We are grateful for his leadership, constructive engagement, and close partnership as we work together toward our shared goal of ending this terrible war and building a secure and prosperous future for Ukraine and Europe," Kushner posted to X .
Merz, speaking to reporters after the meeting, called the China summit a photo-op and said the trilateral format "will not bring peace" in Ukraine.
As he went to shake Putin's hand before an earlier meeting Wednesday on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, Mr. Trump referred to the Russian leader as "my friend."
"Who is he?" the president said, pointing at Putin and smiling. "He's my friend."

articles.title_orig: Dow dives 800 points as Anthropic IPO milestone causes investors to take profits: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow dives 800 points as Anthropic IPO milestone causes investors to take profits: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks tumbled on Thursday, falling to their lows of the session the very moment the widely anticipated artificial intelligence IPO Anthropic began trading .
The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 1.4% after gaining as much as 2% earlier in the session. The S&P 500 shed 1.4%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 822 points, or 1.6%.
Anthropic , trading at the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, opened shortly before noon at $111.50 per share, a 34% pop. The stock was trading more than 10% off the first trading price and was last up 17%.
The major averages fell to session lows immediately following the start of trading for the much-hyped IPO, as investors appeared to take profits at the culmination of this moment for the AI trade.
The artificial intelligence company priced its initial public offering at $83 a share, above the expected range. That had chip stocks and other AI plays jumping in morning trading.
Chipmakers Nvidia and Micron Technology gave up their gains, along with tech giants Microsoft and Meta Platforms . Advanced Micro Devices lost more than 7% after Hunterbrook Capital disclosed a short position in the name, pointing to alleged U.S. export control breaches that involve China.
"This was always going to be a critical test for the tech sector. Anthropic could be the new poster child for AI trade, especially after Nvidia headlines," said Aleks Spencer, Bogart Wealth CIO. "There's a lot here too that needs to be processed and digested, which translates to this period of uncertainty and volatility."
The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) , or Wall Street's so-called fear gauge, reached a day high of close to 29 — its highest level since March — shortly after Anthropic began trading and investors moved out of tech stocks. The index was last above 27.
"The enthusiasm comes in, and it's a great moment to sell the rally and take some profits," Spencer added.
The market has become more cautious on AI as of late, with investors focusing on whether heavy spending on the buildout will translate into meaningful profits. The iShares AI Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) has fallen 10% this month, and embattled AI bellwether Nvidia has dropped 27% while the company grapples with the resignation of its CEO Jensen Huang. Shares of CoreWeave, which had seen its bond yields trade above 16% earlier this month, is down 16% in November.
To be sure, some on Wall Street aren't too alarmed about the rollercoaster ride sparked by Anthropic's debut.
"Today doesn't matter," said Baird tech strategist Ted Mortonson, who deemed the day's action in Anthropic akin to that of a casino. "It's a blink of an eye of their journey. It's an important event, but how they navigate the next three years that will determine valuation."
Anthropic's historic public offering sheds light on how OpenAI's IPO will perform, said Lior Prosor, a managing partner at Deep33, a deep tech venture fund investing in compute, advanced energy and autonomous manufacturing.
"The way capital markets received Anthropic shows that, for premium assets, the market is still very interested in the AI trade," he added. "This is very positive for the rest of the AI industry, from data center builders and the people building turbines for their power to chip providers from Nvidia and AMD to TSMC."
Anthropic opened at $111.50 per share in its Nasdaq debut on Thursday.
While the major indexes took a leg lower immediately after Anthropic began trading at the Nasdaq, Interactive Brokers' chief strategist Steve Sosnick noted that the premarket rally faded before the artificial intelligence giant began trading.
"What we saw before that was the latest round of 'sell the rally' trading that has overtaken the more customary 'buy the dip' in recent days," he said.
Sosnick said that the rationale for the drop wasn't clear, though once the S&P 500 was able to break through a key support level in recent days, 7,300, that's when selling accelerated.
"The dam seemed to break once the big event was behind us," he added.
The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) topped 27 on Thursday, signaling uncertainty in the U.S. market.
It was last hovering at 27.94.
The stock market has been volatile as of late as investors have priced in macreconomic and geopolitical uncertainty. On Thursday, Anthropic listed its shares on the Nasdaq, sparking a selloff that rattled many areas of the market.
The S&P 500 fell further below its 200-day moving average on Thursday as stocks sold off following Anthropic 's initial public offering.
The broad-market index was last hovering around 7,273.98. That puts it about 74 points, or roughly 1%, below its 200-day moving average of 7,348.54.
"That's a big technical signal," Thomas Martin, a partner and senior portfolio manager at Globalt Investments, told CNBC. "It has been above its 200-day moving average for a long time. And, if you're a trend follower, you say, 'okay, well, maybe if it breaks through, you have room to the downside.'"
The S&P 500's latest decline comes one day after its closed below its 200-day moving average for the first time since April 7.
Stocks rolled over to session lows nearly immediately after Anthropic began trading at the Nasdaq. While the AI giant opened 34% higher, it quickly eased from those levels — as enthusiasm around the company's public market debut withered.
The Dow tumbled to trade more than 1,000 points lower, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite were down more than 1% each.
The declines put the Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq all down more than 3% for the month. Per Bespoke, this would be the first November since 2008 that all major indexes are down that much through Nov. 18.
Shares in frontier artificial intelligence laboratory Anthropic opened at $111.50, up 34.3% from its $83 initial public offering price, after raising a record $81 billion in the largest ever sale of stock by a company entering the public market for the first time.
At the opening price, Anthropic, led by CEO Dario Amodei, has a fully diluted market capitalization of roughly $2 trillion. San Francisco-based Anthropic trades on the Nasdaq Stock Market under ticker symbol ANT.
Amodei co-founded Anthropic less than six years ago, in 2021, alongside a handful of other researchers after the group collectively defected from OpenAI.
— Scott Schnipper, Ashley Capoot and Leslie Picker
Anthropic's debut on Thursday will serve as a key measure of just how much investors remain bullish on the artificial intelligence trade.
"It'll be an important barometer for investors' AI appetite," said Callie Cox, director of investment strategy at Plancorp. "AI stocks desperately need some wind at their backs, too ... Wall Street needs a sign that investors still believe in the potential for AI beyond already-elevated expectations."
"The challenge in that thesis is that hot IPOs rarely perform well right out of the gate, especially these days, when every company seems to be vying for a limited pool of capital to fund their AI strategy," she said. "While I wouldn't be surprised to see the stock market take cues from Anthropic's performance, I'd caution investors about trying to read the tea leaves from one event too much."
Enthusiasm around the Anthropic IPO is lifting the broader tech trade, especially those stocks that are direct proxies for the AI company. Here are the latest moves:
JPMorgan downgraded Alphabet corporate bonds to neutral from overweight, noting that "tighter valuations leave less room for outperformance relative to Amazon."
"Our base case assumes strong growth and eventual improvement in cash conversion, but [free cash flow] remains negative through 2028, requiring further financing while substantial liquidity and earnings keep leverage low," wrote credit analyst Erica Spear. "Alphabet's quarter exposed a widening divergence between accelerating Cloud demand and slowing Search growth, with weaker monetization of AI queries adding to uncertainty around the core earnings engine."

articles.title_orig: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
articles.title_zh: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
articles.content_orig:
Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.
Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire deal.
Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.
Wednesday's Israeli incursion deep beyond the Yellow Line was reportedly the first to be publicly announced by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since the ceasefire began.
In the early afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the operation and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety. It also said a section of Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.
In the evening, the IDF said the joint operation with the Shin Bet security service sought "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".
On Thursday morning, Cogat told Palestinians on social media that "the activity has ended, and the Salah al-Din axis has been reopened".
Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".
Gaza's Hamas-run government media office meanwhile said that an estimated 6,000 people had fled their homes and tents because of the operation, and that this amounted to the war crime of forced displacement.
Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed dozens of families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the Israeli evacuation order.
In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man could be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he said.
An image, meanwhile, showed six armoured vehicles, including tanks and bulldozers, around Salah al-Din road.
A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."
"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."
A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".
Asked about those reports, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.
Multiple verified videos of the aftermath of the incursion on Thursday showed destruction, earth banks, and heavy vehicle tracks more than 1.2km beyond the Yellow Line.
That is believed to be the furthest Israeli troops have advanced into central Gaza since they occupied the so-called Netzarim Corridor before the ceasefire.
Some residents returned to check their properties following the Israeli withdrawal.
"The entire area has been destroyed, and we honestly do not know what to do," Abd Aliwa told Reuters news agency as he sat beside a pile of rubble.
Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.
One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second was killed to the north in Gaza City, and the third was killed in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.
The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".
Gaza health officials said another two people were killed on Thursday by Israeli fire in eastern Gaza City, according to Reuters. There was no immediate comment from the IDF.
At least 1,662 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.
Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.
The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.
The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,710 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, its health ministry says.

articles.title_orig: Trump presses European leaders about Ukraine aid in call after Putin summit
articles.title_zh: Trump presses European leaders about Ukraine aid in call after Putin summit
articles.content_orig:
BERLIN — U.S. President Donald Trump called in to a meeting of Ukraine’s European allies on Thursday, according to four European officials who were briefed on the discussion, where he sharply questioned their continued spending on military support for Kyiv.
Hours after concluding a meeting with Kremlin chief Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, Trump called Berlin from Air Force One and said the Russian leader was serious about peace negotiations about Ukraine.
On the call, Trump vigorously expressed his skepticism about further billions in aid being provided to Ukraine by the so-called Coalition of the Willing, according to three of the European officials, who were granted anonymity to describe a private meeting.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
When asked at a press conference following the coalition meeting whether Trump held too rosy a view of Putin’s desire to end the war, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was “quite the opposite” and that Trump had talked about the “horrific” loss of life in the nearly five-year war.
Trump envoy Steve Witkoff, who attended along with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, added: “He sent Jared and I here specifically to be a part of the Coalition of the Willing, and he’s given us instructions on doing everything possible to end this war and be supportive of that effort. And what I heard from him on the call today, was that he mentioned these very same principles to the other two leaders he was meeting with.”
One person who was in the room for the Trump call said the president talked in a general way, and made the point to leaders that a lot of people were dying in this war and countries should stop wasting money on it. Trump also told leaders that Putin is ready to have a negotiation to reach a peace deal, the same person said.
Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz said at the press conference, however, that Europe is providing funding for Ukrainian defense “to enable peace negotiations in the first place and to conduct them from a position of strength.”
Merz added: “We are not providing this strong support to prolong the war. We want to end this war.”
This is a developing story. Alex Gangitano contributed to this report from Washington. James Angelos contributed from Berlin.

WHEN: Today, Thursday, November 19
Below is the unofficial transcript of CNBC's exclusive interview with Anthropic co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei today, Thursday, November 19, following the company's highly anticipated IPO. Following are links to video on CNBC.com: https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/anthropic-ceo-on-scaling-laws-i-dont-think-we-really-believed-it-until-it-actually-happened.html , https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/anthropics-debut-is-one-stop-on-the-journey-says-daniela-amodei.html , https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/dario-amodei-weare-hoping-to-be-investment-grade-in-the-future.html , https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/dario-amodei-on-if-jensen-huang-should-come-back-as-ceo-.html , and https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/anthropic-sibling-founders-reflect-on-ipo-journey.html .
All references must be sourced to CNBC.
ANDREW ROSS SORKIN: Hey, thanks, Carl. Big day here. And I am here with the co-founders of this company, brother and sister. It's an unbelievable story, Dario and Daniela Amodei. Thank you for being here. Congratulations on this big moment.
DANIELA AMODEI: Thank you for having us.
DARIO AMODEI: Thank you for having us.
SORKIN: Here's where I want to start this. When I first met you, you basically just practically started the company. And I'm so curious — you understood scaling laws at the beginning, perhaps better than anybody, but did you ever expect three, four, five years later here we would be and be talking about evaluation that starts with a T?
DARIO AMODEI: You know, the funny thing is, you look at the scaling laws and they're a line on a piece of paper, right? They predict that a model will have certain cognitive capabilities that will be capable of certain economic tasks. But it's one thing to kind of draw that line, and it's a totally different thing to see the consequences out in the world. And so I would say the scaling laws kind of imply that the technology and hopefully our work within it would — would have this scale. But I don't think we really believed it until it actually happened.
SORKIN: And it's happening right now. Daniela, this is now going to be the largest public benefit corporation to go public. What — for those folks who are watching this morning, even thinking about investing in the company, what does that mean, both for the company itself, but also the way investors should think about that?
DANIELA AMODEI: So, as a public benefit corporation, you know, part of why we decided to incorporate this way, is Anthropic mission is so much about how do we build something that is good for everybody? How do we really build for the public benefit? And part of what I think is so interesting about this structure is that we're actually legally required to balance shareholder interest with the public benefit, with the public good. And I think when Dario and I and our other co-founders were starting the organization, you know, we learned about this concept of a public benefit corporation. It really spoke to us, because we said, well, that's exactly what we're trying to do. We're really trying to do something that we do think can have this incredible economic value and impact, but we want it to be baked into essentially our structure that we also have to balance that against building things that are good for people.
SORKIN: OK, so here's the question. How do you balance the idea of growth and the idea of, for example, pacing at this point? This is something you have talked a lot about, pacing, given some of the safety concerns around AI? And how should the investor class think about those competing interests?
DARIO AMODEI: So, this, you know, this is one of the central tensions at the heart of the company. But it's really, because this technology is so powerful, it has so many effects in the world, it's something that every company in this space will have to face, whether they want to or not. We're just facing it more explicitly and more thoughtfully. And so, you think about something like pacing, the idea behind pacing was, you know, imagine that you have — you're driving your car at 60 miles an hour, and then you discover or invent something that could let you drive the car at 200 miles an hour, right? This is models building themselves, recursive self-improvement. What we have done with pacing is essentially said, look, you know, we could drive at 200 miles an hour. Maybe let's only drive at 90 miles an hour, spend time figuring out how to do that safely, and the rest of that surplus, we spend building the model in the right way. And you know, I think, in the long run, that will work out pretty well for the investors as well, because the company that builds the safest, that has trust of the customers and the enterprises of the world, I think that is the company that's going to be both best for society and, in the long run, I hope, best for the performance of the company. And I think that's what we often look for. We look for synergies, ways to make the two line up in the long run.
SORKIN:  What does success look like today? When we see the price of this, do you say to yourself, if this is up 10 percent, 20 percent, that's success? If it's up too much, is that not success? What does, I mean, you guys have spent a lot of time with your bankers and—
DARIO AMODEI:  I think that's one of the very few topics we're not allowed to talk about.
DANIELA AMODEI:  I think, you know, I think maybe the way I would put it is, Anthropic has always been a very long-term-focused company, right? We have always been thinking about, how is this technology going to be beneficial to people in the future, but also what can it do for people today? And so while today is a super exciting milestone and we're obviously really, really excited about it, I think it's, for us, it's like one stop on the journey, right? We think about this as, wow, this is an incredible moment for Anthropic, for our mission, but we're going to wake up tomorrow and we're going to be the same company. And I think that's really, at least for me, what I have been focusing on today.
SORKIN:  The rate of growth of this company has been extraordinary, but I want to understand the unlock and also understand the competition in the space, because, increasingly, you have open-weight models. You have competitors in OpenAI, which are trying to offer tokens at cheaper prices. You have folks like Microsoft, which offer your services, and yet are also trying to sell their own models. And they say oftentimes that some of those models, or at least some of the features of their models, can do some of the same things, maybe not at the frontier level. How do you think about that in terms of what that means longer term to the margins for the company?
DARIO AMODEI:  So, I think, I think a couple concepts. One concept is the frontier. And we have found that there are these incredible returns to the frontier. And in most products or goods, you have competition on price. Here, the competition is really on quality, because the returns to greater cognitive ability are so high, right? As we climb the exponential of cognitive ability, you go from doing chatbots, to being able to do coding, to being able to do biology and robotics. And the economic value of things further along the frontier is so much larger than things earlier in the frontier that that's where most of the value accumulates. The second idea is that, if you're good at the frontier, you are also good at producing smaller and more efficient models away from the frontier. So, if you look at Haiku 5.5, we were able to drop the price by 4X from Haiku 4.5 and by many times from Opus and Fable 5 family, which are, which it's, which it's much cheaper than. And so we are able to also compete using our, the same technology that we build our models, models on the frontier, the same compute multipliers, to make these cheap models that compete away from the frontier.

articles.title_orig: U.N. Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
articles.title_zh: U.N. Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
articles.content_orig:
Rohingya genocide: What was said in court and what happens now?
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.
Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
Rohingyas at the Cox's Bazar camp in Bangladesh, where around a million refugees now reside, watched the verdict live
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.
After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.
Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.
The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
Watch: Genocide judgement will 'mean a great deal' for Rohingya community
Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.
He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.
Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.
While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there was "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.
Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.
In January, government representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.
The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.
It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.
The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."
Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".
Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".
To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.
Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.
Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest of crimes under international law.
Rohingya refugees were seen reacting as the ICJ verdict was broadcast on a big screen in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh
Philippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment".
He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.
However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.
The ruling will, though, have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.
Sands said that pending case had been the "elephant in the room" during the Myanmar hearings.
He added that, while ruling against Myanmar did not mean the court would find similarly with Gaza, if it had not found Myanmar responsible, the case against Israel "would, in effect, be over". Israel says the case against it is "wholly unfounded".
ICJ president Yuji Iwasawa said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population
Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, told the BBC that the court had not accepted Myanmar's counter-terrorism defence and had found for the first time that rape and sexual violence was an act of genocide, positions it would bear in mind for future cases.
A spokesperson for the US State Department said "the proper interpretation" of the Genocide Convention is of "paramount importance", and so is "preventing politicisation" of the International Criminal Court. "We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications," they said.
They said they share the "grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups", and added the US is the "leading donor for the Rohingya refugee humanitarian response".
Following Thursday's ruling, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the government was ordering Myanmar's defence attachÃ© be expelled and that he was summoning its charge d'affaires.
He pledged to set out "further action in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held to account" after a cross-party group of MPs called for the government to resume sanctions against Myanmar's military.

articles.title_orig: AMD sheds nearly $100 billion in market value as China chip concerns hit AI stocks
articles.title_zh: AMD sheds nearly $100 billion in market value as China chip concerns hit AI stocks
articles.content_orig:
Concerns about balance sheets and valuations in the artificial intelligence sector have hit the market hard since October, and investors who have shorted publicly traded tech companies in the AI trade have profited. Most investors don't think as much about "shorting" debt, but there will be a way through exchange-traded funds to profit from widening credit default swap spreads of top AI companies.
Both Tuttle Capital and Defiance ETFs have filed for funds that target the credit default swaps of companies closely linked to the AI trade, from CoreWeave and Oracle to the Magnificent Seven: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms, Microsoft Corporation, Nvidia, Tesla, and Apple.
Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier. CDS is a closely watched indicator of issuer health in the debt markets, especially in the AI market this year. The ETFs are designed to gain when the CDS spreads of these companies widen, either as a group in the case of a Magnificent Seven CDS fund, or individually in the case of proposed ETFs targeting Oracle, CoreWeave and Meta. The funds would lose value when the market assesses the creditworthiness of these debt issuers as improving.
Both ETF managers filed for CoreWeave and Oracle CDS funds, specifically, among broader AI and semiconductor company CDS portfolios.
If the exchange-traded fund managers get approval from the Securities and Exchange Commission, these portfolios would be the first of their kind in an ETF market that has become more aggressive in recent years about launching higher-risk strategies revolving around more complex financial instruments than just public stocks and bonds. The ETF managers plan to employ leverage in the portfolios, which both increases risk and the potential for outsized returns on any given day, similar to the way existing single-stock leverage and inverse ETFs function.
The ETF managers say these CDS funds can serve an important role in a market on edge about AI debt.
"As AI infrastructure investment accelerates and companies take on significant capital commitments to fund that growth, we see an opportunity to give investors more targeted tools to manage credit risk and hedge potential financial stress across some of the biggest names driving the AI buildout," Sylvia Jablonski, CIO of Defiance ETFs, said in a statement to CNBC.
Neocloud companies like CoreWeave are a major focus for AI skeptics, an AI bubble watch compounded by the exit of Jensen Huang from Nvidia, who is seen as a critical player in financing the AI buildout, with Nvidia called by some the "central bank of AI ."
Apollo Global Management CEO Marc Rowan on Tuesday said that neocloud company AI projects could face an existential crisis if Nvidia funding dries up. "There was a strong incentive for Nvidia as a business matter to get these projects off the ground," Rowan said in an interview with CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ." "If that banking function, that guarantor function, gets taken away, access to capital for a large number of neoclouds is going to disappear."
In its earnings filings and conference call on Tuesday, Nvidia shifted the tone in discussing the way it finances the AI ecosystem.
Matthew Tuttle, founder and CEO of Tuttle Capital Management, said it is less likely that these ETFs will find an audience among retail investors than smaller institutional players.
"It may be a stretch for the average retail guy," he said, but he added that having managed leveraged and inverse ETFs, it is clear that many investors "get interested" when a particular asset is seeing outsized moves, as has been the case with AI company-linked CDS in 2026. "The stuff that moves a lot is the stuff that tends to generate the most interest," he said.
Both prospectuses stress that these funds are not designed to move inversely to the reference companies' stocks and can lose money while a company's shares decline. They also note these funds don't short bonds or bet directly against a company's stock, and to buy CDS protection, they pay premiums, which are a unique cost to the fund manager whether or not credit conditions worsen.
The CDS of these companies have been on the move in a major way as part of the AI trade over the past year.
CoreWeave's 9.75% bond due in 2031 is yielding close to 16%, while spreads on its five-year credit default swaps were recently between 1,100-1,200. Spreads over 1,000 are generally considered a sign of distress.
CoreWeave executives have taken their messaging about the debt public, with co-founder and chief strategy officer Brian Venturo posting on X.com on Wednesday that he had purchased $30 million in unsecured company bonds and was going to hold them until maturity in 2031. "I've never been more confident in CoreWeave," he wrote.
Oracle CDS contracts have moved up over the past year from below 80 to a current range above 300.
The CDS spreads on the biggest tech companies, including Amazon and Meta as examples, rose over 100% within the past year, as their free cash flow turned negative from spending heavily on AI. Even though the market is much less concerned about their balance sheets than that of the neoclouds, major tech company CDS spreads did hit five-year highs earlier this month.
Tuttle said that these ETFs, if approved, would be the "easiest" to use for smaller institutions and family offices that want CDS exposure and "are either too small to trade with the Goldmans of the world or lack the in-house expertise to trade CDS on their own."
"It is a different way to hedge the AI trade," Tuttle said.
ETF investing experts expressed skepticism about this approach and market reception. "I don't see much demand materializing for these types of products," said Nate Geraci, president of NovaDius Wealth Management. But he added it does make sense to target these ETFs "at retail investors who are seeing scary headlines around AI capex spending. Yet another way to speculate (gamble)," he said.
Todd Sohn, chief ETF strategist at Baird Strategas, said he foresees confusion with how these funds will work. "How many non-professionals know what CDS are?" he said.
Tuttle says it won't take billions in assets to make an ETF focused on AI CDS a minor financial success. "My criteria is I want to see a runway to $20 million, which is about our breakeven. I see it here. It doesn't mean it will happen, but I think we have a decent chance."
— CNBC's Michelle Fox contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
articles.title_zh: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global powerbroker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. He made an appeal for regional harmony, saying: “Members of Apec are like passengers riding the same ship. To navigate the waves of the Pacific, we must unite as one and look out for each other.”
However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – with the US president calling the Russian his “friend”. The peace declaration said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

"There is no disruption to our services," according to the statement.
JPMorganChase said Thursday morning that "third parties who provide services" to the banking giant "were the target of a cyberattack."
"Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," the statement continued.
"There is no disruption to our services," according to the statement.
JPMorganChase, the largest U.S. bank, did not disclose when the cyberattack occurred or name the third-party companies that were targeted.
"Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring," the company said in its statement.
The company added that it found "no connection to service disruptions some customers experienced earlier this week."
JPMorganChase said on Monday that it experienced technical issues that triggered online delays across several major U.S. banks. Chase blamed the outage on a "software bug."
There have been several recent tech outages across the nation that affected air travel, email and hotel reservations, and even slowed classified internal communications at the National Security Agency.
Top Trump administration officials continued this week to insist that there is no evidence that those outages were the result of cyberattacks.

articles.title_orig: Chinese tech firms fear AI hits from US curbs after Nvidia fallout
articles.title_zh: Chinese tech firms fear AI hits from US curbs after Nvidia fallout
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Chinese technology firms are bracing for impacts on their ambitious artificial intelligence plans as the U.S. tightens restrictions on China 's access to the world's cutting-edge chips.
Chinese tech giant Alibaba , which on Thursday announced another quarter of strong revenue growth for its global AI cloud and compute services, warned that the new U.S. rules could affect some of its global data center expansion plans. It said it was still assessing the repercussions.
The Trump administration this week issued new rules in the wake of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, following the news that he’d had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
The rules now restrict remote computing access through data centers in third countries, the latest U.S. move to curtail China’s abilities to use advanced Nvidia chips to train its increasingly capable AI models.
Alibaba's AI revenues are surging as demand grows
As the technology race between the two superpowers intensifies, existing U.S. export restrictions already barred China from getting the world’s most powerful chips.
But some Chinese companies have been able to bypass those restrictions by renting remote computing access to train AI models, pushing the U.S. to close what some policymakers called a loophole.
As global AI usage grows, Alibaba has been expanding its capabilities across chips, cloud infrastructure and AI models. It launched its flagship Qwen4-Max AI model earlier this week. In September, Alibaba's CEO called its new Zhenwu V900 chip the “most powerful” AI chip in China, while it announced massive data center investment plans in China and abroad.
Alibaba Cloud’s AI-related revenue currently comes significantly from China and there’s still a lot of “untapped demand” from Chinese enterprises, said Jacob Cooke of the Beijing-based consultancy WPIC Marketing + Technologies.
For the latest July-September quarter, Alibaba reported a 53% year-on-year revenue surge for its AI cloud and compute services to nearly 61 billion yuan ($9 billion). Total revenue for the quarter rose 10% from the year before to almost 272 billion yuan ($41 billion), slightly better than what analysts had expected.
While the company has a strong cash buffer, capital expenditures jumped 60% during the quarter to 50.5 billion yuan ($7.6 billion) thanks to its increased spending on AI infrastructure buildout.
Tencent says US chip curb ‘sets everyone back in China’
Chinese tech giant Tencent on Wednesday said the new U.S. rule on chip access “sets everyone back in China.”
“Everyone is actually having less compute, advanced compute, to work with, no matter when you actually started leasing or building capacities outside of China,” Tencent President Martin Lau said on an earnings call. Training timelines for Tencent’s next versions of its AI models would probably be impacted, he said.
“Chinese AI firms are still heavily dependent on the most frontier Nvidia chips," said James Chai, a researcher at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, with new U.S. rules on remote access cutting off a huge portion of Chinese firms’ access to compute.
A study released in October by the Institute for Progress, a U.S. think tank, estimated that remote access to AI chips through overseas data centers could account for roughly one-third of China’s AI compute by the end of 2027.
Nvidia, meanwhile, said it is now “no longer shipping” chips including the H200, one of its more powerful chips, though not the most advanced, although the Trump administration greenlighted some sales to China, reflecting how Nvidia has toughened its stance on China following Huang’s ouster.
Analysts expect the U.S. will step up its chip export control policies against China after Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former senior executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, raised U.S. national security concerns. Earlier reporting by The New York Times suggested that U.S. officials suspected Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited in part to potentially influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available to Chinese companies.
Beijing has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, and has called the new U.S. rules blocking Chinese companies' remote access to computing power overseas “economic coercion.”
Analysts and industry leaders in China say the U.S.’s tightening of chip export control measures would ultimately accelerate China’s push to make its domestic chip industry self-sufficient.
“Over the longer run, we believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips, which we actually see the industry is actually progressing very fast,” said Tencent's Lau.

articles.title_orig: As Burnham heads to Brussels, are new Brexit wars about to begin?
articles.title_zh: As Burnham heads to Brussels, are new Brexit wars about to begin?
articles.content_orig:
Lincolnshire, United Kingdom – A decade is a short time in cheesemaking. Barrels of Tim Jones’ “Lincolnshire Poachers” cheese rest on their racks for months and years, disturbed only by Florence, the robot cheese turner.
Complexity, depth and flavour develop with patience.
The most mature cheese in Tim’s Lincolnshire dairy, in the English midlands, is five years old. By that measure, it was only a couple of cheeses ago that 52 percent of the British public voted for the country’s most tumultuous constitutional revolt in living memory.
Jones was one of them. But he is under no illusion that it went well – particularly for his exports.
“It suddenly made life much harder. We lost certain customers, and it became more expensive to get the cheese there. It definitely harmed our business,” he told Al Jazeera.
Ten years after the UK voted to leave the European Union, few are happy with what they got.
Remainers are still heartbroken that a majority of the country did not look on EU membership with approval. Leavers, by and large, think many of Brexit’s promised benefits were never delivered.
“I did vote to leave,” said Jones. “But I didn’t vote to leave in the way that we did.”
Recent polling tells a consistent story: A majority of Britons now view Brexit as a mistake.
In September, 55 percent of respondents told YouGov that leaving the EU was a wrong turn for the UK. Only 21 percent think it was the right decision.
Fifty-nine percent of Britons now support rejoining the EU.
The relatively new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has noticed the shift in public mood. Less cautious than his predecessor, Keir Starmer, Burnham reignited the Brexit debate shortly after taking office in July.
He has ruled out major changes to the UK’s relationship with the EU before the next general election. But he would like to see the country back in the bloc within his lifetime, and has suggested that a future Labour manifesto could promise a new referendum.
The changing mood is only part of the logic. A government searching for growth would naturally prioritise what is still its biggest trade partner. Geopolitics matter too. The UK’s bond with the United States is less reliable than it was.
Unsurprisingly, Brexit talk has swept through media in Britain and, to a lesser extent, in Europe. Burnham insists he will not get ahead of the public on this. His immediate concern, he says, is improving the current UK-EU relationship.
On Friday, Burnham will be in Brussels for the second UK-EU Summit – a vehicle established under Starmer to deepen post-Brexit cooperation.
Among the deals being worked on are a youth mobility scheme, an emissions trading agreement, and a food and drink trade deal.
Jones, the Lincolnshire cheesemaker, is hopeful.
“If he can reduce the red tape and the cost of sending cheese to Europe – and for us that means across the world – that would be a huge positive for us,” he said – although he was less certain which way he would vote in another referendum.
“Gosh, I genuinely don’t know. I think it would depend entirely on a critical view on the arguments that were presented at the time. A much more critical view than I had the first time around.”
It is an issue familiar to anyone who has lived through the Brexit years: the terms matter.
Former premier Theresa May used the motto, “Brexit means Brexit”. But the slogan was vague. What kind of Brexit? Hard? Soft? Norway Plus? Canada Plus?
There were many potential Brexits – as there might be many possible ways to rejoin.
Some are more popular than others.
A new YouGov survey gave people a menu of 18 options.
In the most popular scenario, 58 percent said they would vote to rejoin if the UK stayed out of the euro, joined the border-free Schengen Zone, and kept its previous rebate from the EU budget. But if the UK lost the rebate, did not join Schengen, and adopted the euro, only 35 percent of people said they would be interested in EU membership.
Anticipating the battles ahead, two pro-Brexit campaign groups are relaunching under new names: Stay Out and Enough Official.
Burnham says he will begin talks with the EU about options for the long-term relationship after this week’s summit.
Buckle up, the Brexit wars may be starting again.

A "terrorist attack" by the Iran-backed Houthis damaged multiple floors at the tallest skyscraper in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, which houses the headquarters of the Saudi Public Investment Fund on Thursday, authorities and reports said.
Entrances leading into the King Abdullah Financial District were closed and people were being evacuated from the area following the strike by a suspected Houthi missile, according to Reuters.
The news agency reported that the attack on the Public Investment Fund Tower, which is 80 stories tall, destroyed windows across up to eight floors of the building and bent portions of its metal facade.
"One of the towers of the Financial Center in Riyadh was targeted in a terrorist attack by the terrorist Houthi militia, causing material damage but no injuries — praise be to God," the General Directorate of Saudi Civil Defense wrote on X as it shared a photo of the damage.
HOUTHIS KILL 14 AT SAUDI AIRPORT AS EXPERT WARNS OF 'RAPID TARGETS' AMID MIDDLE EAST WAR
The Public Investment Fund Tower in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, is the tallest skyscraper in the city. The building was seen damaged on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, following what officials called a "terrorist attack" by the Iran-backed Houthis. (General Directorate of Saudi Civil Defense)
The incident unfolded after the Houthis attacked a building belonging to Saudi state-owned oil company Aramco, in the same area on Nov. 8, Reuters reported.
Saudi-led coalition spokesman Col. Turki Al-Malki said Thursday that Saudi air defenses "intercepted and destroyed 4 ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia toward the southern region."
He also said the coalition went on offense in Yemen, destroying a ballistic missile launch platform in Dhamar that was used by the Houthis "in an attempt to attack Riydah today."

The Houthis have been escalating attacks on Saudi Arabia during the U.S.-Iran war.
The U.S. Embassy and Consulates in Saudi Arabia warned Americans earlier this week that they "should exercise heightened vigilance due to the increased threat of armed attacks by Iranian-supported Houthis and Iranian efforts to target U.S. government officials and facilities in the region.

Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices were down about 7% Wednesday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."
Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.
The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."
The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.
AMD did not immediately reply to a CNBC request for comment.
Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, said on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine strikes Putin’s prized Crimean bridge for third time in a week
articles.title_zh: Ukraine strikes Putin’s prized Crimean bridge for third time in a week
articles.content_orig:
Russian president makes remarks after Ukraine strikes strategic bridge to Crimea for third time in a week
Vladimir Putin has said Russia’s response to the bombing of the Kerch bridge to Crimea will be “painful”, after Ukraine attacked the strategic connection for the third time this week.
The warning was delivered at a press conference after Putin met Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China. The Russian president claimed he had been considering agreeing to local ceasefires until the Kerch road bridge was destroyed.
“After the strikes on the Crimean Bridge, we will not negotiate,” Putin said, insisting the bridge was used only by civilians. “We will respond to these attacks. Our response will be far more painful than Kyiv’s attack on the bridge.”
A series of explosions were heard in the Ukrainian capital in the mid-afternoon, and there were reports that a Russian drone had struck near the Dutch embassy in Kyiv, though it was unclear if it was deliberately targeted.
Shortly after midnight on Tuesday, Ukraine’s military blew up the central span of the Kerch road bridge in a complex air raid that involved Ruta cruise missiles made by a Dutch company as well as several Ukrainian cruise missiles and drones.
Russia threatened the Netherlands afterwards, with the Russian embassy in the country asking: “Is the Dutch government openly taking part in the conflict?” after the company, Destinus, had said it was a key element in the attack.
Tom Berendsen, the Dutch foreign minister, confirmed that “a projectile struck behind” the embassy in Kyiv. “Fortunately, our colleagues are unharmed, though there is some minor damage to the building,” he said, adding that officials were now investigating the incident.
A 26-year-old man had been killed and five others injured in the afternoon attacks, city authorities said.
Ukrainian military sources said the destruction of the Kerch bridge had been deliberately timed to embarrass Putin before the extraordinary summit , in which the Russian president sat down with Trump and Xi to discuss the war and other issues.
After his talks with Putin, Trump dialled into a meeting of Ukraine’s European allies in Berlin, during which he reportedly asked why European countries continued to spend billions on military support for Kyiv and said Putin was ready to negotiate a peace deal.
The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, when asked at a press conference whether Trump was painting too optimistic a picture of Russia’s desire for peace, said: “Too rosy a picture? No, certainly not. That was not the phone call that we heard from the president this afternoon. I would say quite the opposite, to be honest.”
Ukraine followed up Tuesday’s bombing of the Kerch bridge with a further attack on the remaining rail bridge to Crimea on Wednesday night. Train services were halted as a result of the strikes, which Ukraine’s military said were conducted with Neptune missiles made in Ukraine.
Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, said on Wednesday night that there had been another attack on the bridge, then added on Thursday that trains would start crossing from “approximately 4pm”.
Emergency repair workers had made “heroic efforts” to restore the track, the governor said. Nobody was reported wounded as a result of the incident, Russia’s transport ministry added.
Ukraine’s military said the Kerch bridge was “the main land artery the Russian army uses to supply its occupation groupings in the south with fuel, ammunition and equipment” – in contrast to the comments made by Putin.
The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) bridge, built by Russia after its occupation of Crimea, has been struck three times in a week. Initial attacks on Monday had shown that Tuesday’s full-scale assault would be possible.
A 227-metre section of the road spanning the Kerch strait collapsed into the Sea of Azov after a complex air raid that had been prepared and planned over several weeks.
A source in Ukraine’s armed forces said this week’s attacks were designed to embarrass Putin on the world stage. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” they said.
For Ukraine, the bridge across the Kerch strait is a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Ukraine has previously declared that the bridge, built eight years ago, is illegal. Kyiv had tried to blow it up twice in the past – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.
Zelesnkyy described the earlier attack this week as the culmination of a seven-stage campaign to demolish the bridge, largely involving domestically produced drones and ballistic missiles, clearing the radar and air defences of Russian-occupied Ukraine.
Flamingo FP-5 cruise missiles and Palianytsia drones struck the central section of the bridge, bringing down its supporting arch.

articles.title_orig: Social Security raise: What’s left after the Medicare premium hike?
articles.title_zh: Social Security raise: What’s left after the Medicare premium hike?
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Medicare, which provides health insurance coverage to roughly 75 million retired seniors and disabled workers in the US, is getting more expensive next year.
Medicare Part B premiums, which cover doctors, outpatient care, some home healthcare services, and durable medical equipment, will rise about 3.2% to $209.40 a month in 2027, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) announced Tuesday .
That's an increase of $6.50 a month from $202.90 in 2026, bringing the total premium to $2,512.80 a year.
The Medicare Part B premium is deducted from your Social Security checks before you receive them. The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2027 . Starting in January, the increase will add an average of $75 per month.
That is great news, but the Medicare premium increase will eat into it.
The annual deductible for all Medicare Part B beneficiaries increases to $292 in 2027, up $9 from $283 in 2026.
The increase in the standard premium and deductible is mainly due to projected increases in healthcare spending, according to CMS.
"The increase in the Medicare Part B premium for 2027 is less than the much steeper 10% increase in 2026, so that's a bit of good news," said Juliette Cubanski, director of the program on Medicare policy at KFF.
"Still, this increase comes on top of rising costs for other Medicare benefits, including prescription drugs, plus rising costs for other everyday essentials," she added.
Read more: How to add or adjust your Medicare coverage
People with traditional Medicare generally pay the Part B premium for physician coverage and a separate one for prescription drug coverage, known as Part D. Those premiums vary by plan. Some people pay an additional monthly premium for inpatient hospital coverage (Part A).
Each year, the Medicare Part B premium, deductible, and coinsurance rates are reset. If you're enrolled in traditional Medicare, you also have a Part D drug plan. The 2027 Part D base premium is $36 per month on average, but yours could be higher.
"Americans clearly understand that healthcare costs can threaten their retirement security," Kelly LaVigne, vice president of Consumer Insights at Allianz Life, told Yahoo Finance. But "so many don't fully understand what Medicare will and won't cover. And the details matter."
Roughly 15% of the average retiree's annual expenses will be health-related, according to Fidelity. On average, a 65-year-old who leaves the workforce this year may need $185,500 in savings to cover out-of-pocket healthcare expenses throughout retirement.
Even though the program offers fairly comprehensive coverage, traditional Medicare does not have an annual out-of-pocket limit.
The biggest hardship for many people enrolled in original Medicare is that Part B pays only 80% of expenses.
To cover the rest, you need to purchase a Medigap health insurance policy, sold by private insurers, that covers the remaining expenses.
For Medicare and Medicare Advantage users looking to make changes to their plans, the open enrollment period for 2027 ends Dec. 7.
Kerry Hannon is a Senior Columnist at Yahoo Finance. She is a career and retirement strategist and the author of 14 books, including " Retirement Bites: A Gen X Guide to Securing Your Financial Future, " " In Control at 50+: How to Succeed in the New World of Work ," and "Never Too Old to Get Rich.

articles.title_orig: Stocks making the biggest moves Thursday: Palo Alto Networks, Take-Two Interactive, Everpure, Walmart & more
articles.title_zh: Stocks making the biggest moves Thursday: Palo Alto Networks, Take-Two Interactive, Everpure, Walmart & more
articles.content_orig:
Palo Alto Networks popped in early trading Thursday, boosted by quarterly results that beat analyst expectations. AMD, meanwhile, tumbled on the back of a short seller report.
Follow along as CNBC covers the biggest stock market moves of the day.
Neocloud CoreWeave gained 1% on enthusiasm from the Anthropic IPO plus a change in Texas permitting that favors data center development.
Texas officials started issuing air permits again for data center construction projects, according to Reuters , which bodes well for the future of the physical component of the AI buildout.
Nvidia's highly anticipated earnings call earlier this week also offered clarity on the leadership direction for the firm, which Wall Street analysts responded positively to. Analysts at Truist were encouraged on Tuesday by Nvidia statements on the call about its relationship to neoclouds.
"Notably, NVIDIA's earnings commentary … [described] neoclouds as an 'increasingly important' part of the global AI infrastructure ecosystem and stating that it will continue working with and supporting leading neocloud partners, while becoming more disciplined and selective in that support."
AMD shares tumbled more than 9% after Hunterbrook Capital revealed it took a short position on the company.
In a post titled "AMD has its own China problem", Hunterbrook alleges that "AMD firmware keeps turning up at a blacklisted Chinese company and three companies tied to it, just as U.S. export restrictions are scheduled to expand."
"AMD, which bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong, also depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips," Hunterbrook added.
CNBC reached out to AMD for comment.
Shares of Coherent are up nearly 11%, extending gains after Nvidia 's latest earnings report earlier in the week highlighted continued demand for data-center technology.
Coherent, which supplies optical components used in AI data centers, said its data-center revenue rose 85% year over year in its fiscal first quarter.
On Nov. 18, the company's board authorized a share repurchase program of up to $2 billion . Coherent may buy shares in the open market or through other transactions. The program has no expiration date and does not require the company to repurchase a specific amount.
Shares of the software company making tools for computer chips jumped 3.2% after Barclays initiated coverage with an overweight rating and a $640 price target implying 47% upside from Wednesday's close. Analyst Saket Kalia noted that Synopsys is the leader of a growing Electronic Design Automation (EDA) market, which is driven by rising spend in semiconductor research and development.
MongoDB gained 4% before the bell following an upgrade at UBS to buy from neutral.
The bank's channel checks pointed to steady demand and better-than-expected consumer and partner growth, which should support durable 20%-plus total revenue growth and 25%-plus revenue growth for its cloud database service Atlas over the coming years, analyst Radi Sultan said.
In addition, MongoDB could be utilized in 20% to 40% of incremental AI workloads, which is not fully reflected in the stock's valuation, he said.
Data storage stocks are getting a lift in the premarket Thursday as the Anthropic IPO aims to breathe new life into AI-trade
Shares of Seagate Technology are up more than 6% while Western Digital stock popped 5.8%.
Seagate and Western Digital provide provide mass data storage infrastructure, a crucial role in the AI ecosystem to help AI models run.
The strong momentum around data storage and AI infrastructure demand is already high.
But a large chuck of that demand will come from leading AI lab Anthropic, which is set to go public Thursday.
Chipmakers advanced on Thursday ahead of Anthropic's IPO.
Marvell gained 4.2%, Advanced Micro Devices is up 2.8%, Broadcom advanced 2.5%, Intel moved 4.4% higher and Nvidia is up 1.5%.
These artificial intelligence chips will help Anthropic run Claude models faster.
Leading chipmakers need the IPO to go well, as Anthropic has $900 billion in spending commitments.
Shares of Bloom Energy surged nearly 8% in the premarket Thursday after being upgraded to outperform at BMO Capital Markets.
The analysts cited their endorsement of the company after coming away with positive meetings with management.
The firm however decreased its price target to $230 from $260, which still implies a 35% upside to the stock's Thursday close of $170 per share.
UBS upgraded the intelligent content management provider to buy from neutral, sending shares 3.6% higher in premarket trading.
The firm believes Box 's recent artificial intelligence growth acceleration can support sustained double-digit revenue growth. "Investors have been looking for evidence that AI can drive an inflection in software growth, and Box is increasingly demonstrating exactly that," analyst Taylor McGinnis wrote.
Walmart shares were down more than 1% even after the retail giant reported third-quarter results that beat expectations and raised its full-year guidance.
The company posted adjusted earnings per share of 65 cents on revenue of $188.84 billion. Analysts expected a profit of 64 cents per share on revenue of $187.27 billion.
For the year, Walmart sees net sales rising 4.9% to 5.2%, more than a previous guidance of 4% to 5%.
Shares of Take-Two Interactive slipped 1%, giving back some of their gains from the previous session. The stock popped more than 6% on Wednesday ahead of the release of the much-anticipated "Grand Theft Auto VI" game.
Take-Two is up nearly 14% in November, though the stock has dropped 15% in 2026.
Cybersecurity player Palo Alto Networks advanced 10% after its fiscal first-quarter results came in above the Street's expectations.
The company earned $1.05 per share on an adjusted basis and revenue of $3.44 billion. The LSEG consensus estimate called for 97 cents per share on $3.31 billion of revenue.
Guidance for the fiscal year ending July 2027 calls for adjusted earnings of $4.26 to $4.30 per share on revenue of $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion. Analysts sought $4.18 per share and $14.16 billion, according to LSEG.
The data management company advanced 5% after raising its guidance for the fiscal-year ending January 2027.
Everpure sees revenue in a range of $5.20 billion to $5.21 billion, up from its earlier call of $5.03 billion to $5.07 billion. Analysts polled by FactSet were looking for $5.06 billion.
Third-quarter results also surpassed estimates on the top and bottom lines.
The manufacturer of power generation equipment pulled back 1%. Woodward expects adjusted earnings for the fiscal year ending September 2027 to range between $10.20 and $10.70 per share, below the FactSet consensus estimate of $10.74 per share.
